cse.title: Stock market
cse.intro: The Colombo Stock Exchange's session in numbers: indices, activity, foreign flows and breadth.
cse.headline: Headline indices
cse.averagePending: 20-session average available after {count, plural, one {# more session} other {# more sessions}}
cse.valuation: Market valuation (as published by the CSE)
cse.breadthNote: Ordinary voting and non-voting shares that traded, against their previous close.
cse.moversNote: Among shares with turnover of at least Rs 1 mn this session.
cse.noTurnover: The CSE's turnover figures for this session were not collected (the session was filled in from the price history), so the most-traded list and the largest moves are not shown.
cse.leadLong: The Colombo Stock Exchange's day in one page: where the indices closed, how much traded, how many shares rose and fell, what foreign investors did, and which shares moved most.

sections.indicesWhy: An index sums up the market in one number. The ASPI covers every listed company, weighted by size; the S&P SL20 follows 20 large, frequently traded companies.
sections.indicesHow: Read the change against recent days rather than on its own: a 1% day is large on the CSE. When the ASPI and the S&P SL20 move apart, the largest companies are moving differently from the rest.
sections.activityWhy: Turnover shows how much money changed hands. A move on heavy turnover reflects many investors; on light turnover, a few trades can move prices.
sections.activityHow: Compare each figure with its 20-session average, shown under it: 1.5× means half again as much as usual.
sections.breadthWhy: Breadth shows whether a move was shared by most companies or driven by a few large ones. Foreign investors' net flow shows whether money from abroad came in or went out.
sections.breadthHow: An index can rise while more shares fall than rise, when a few large companies go up. Foreign flows on one day can come from a single large trade; look at them over several days.
sections.valuationWhy: These figures relate the whole market's price to its companies' combined profits, net assets and dividends, as the CSE publishes them.
sections.valuationHow: Compare them with the market's own history and with government bond yields: a dividend yield well below the treasury bill yield means investors are counting on growth.
sections.movers: Most traded, largest rises and falls
sections.moversWhy: The day's most traded shares show where investors' attention was; the largest moves show which prices changed most.
sections.moversHow: Large percentage moves on small turnover can be a single trade, so the lists of rises and falls include only shares with meaningful turnover.
sections.sectorsWhy: Sector indices show which parts of the economy the market's moves came from: banks, consumer companies, manufacturing and so on.
sections.sectorsHow: A sector with few companies can move sharply on one company's news; check the share pages behind a large sector move.

shares.title: Shares
shares.intro: Every share's latest session. Prices are as published and are not adjusted for splits, bonuses or rights; a flag marks where that matters.
shares.rangePosHelp: Where the close sits between the 52-week low (0%) and high (100%) the CSE publishes.
shares.relHelp: Price return minus the ASPI's return over 5, 21 and 63 sessions.
shares.flagJump: A move of more than 40% in one session inside this window: probably a corporate action the prices are not adjusted for.
shares.flagNoTrade: No trade before the start of this window.
shares.flagRange: A move of more than 40% in one session within the last year: the 52-week range may not be comparable.
shares.ratiosHelp: P/E, P/B and dividend yield of the company, at the voting share's close (from the companies' interim reports; blank where the figures do not reconcile).
shares.why: One table for every listed share, so a company can be found and compared with the rest of the market: its latest price, how it moved against the ASPI, and its valuation figures.
shares.how: Sort by any column by selecting its heading. Returns against the ASPI show whether a share's price did better or worse than the market over the same period. P/E, P/B and dividend yield come from each company's latest interim report; compare them between similar companies rather than across the whole market. Select a share for its full page.
shares.introBySector: Every company listed on the Colombo Stock Exchange, grouped by industry. Type part of a company's name or its symbol to find it, or choose a sector; open a sector to see its companies.
shares.compareIntro: Every listed share in one table, sortable by any column: price change, turnover, returns against the ASPI and company figures.
shares.compareLink: Compare all shares in one sortable table
shares.searchPlaceholder: Company or symbol, e.g. John Keells or JKH
shares.sectorSum: {count, plural, one {# share} other {# shares}} · today {up} rose, {down} fell · median change {median}
shares.noMatch: No share matches. Try part of the company's name, or its symbol.
shares.howBySector: Companies are grouped into the 20 industry groups the CSE's sector indices use, alphabetically within each. Each sector's line shows how many of its shares rose and fell today and the median change. P/E and dividend yield come from each company's latest interim report; compare them within a sector rather than across the market. For sorting by any figure, use the comparison table.

dealings.title: Directors' dealings
dealings.intro: Listed companies must tell the CSE when one of their directors deals in the company's shares, in the director's own name or through a related party. These are those disclosures as the CSE published them, usually one to four market days after the dealing. They record what happened; they say nothing about what a share's price will do.
dealings.namesNote: Names are shown as the companies filed them with the CSE; each dealing links to its notice on the CSE's website.
dealings.recentNote: The {count} most recent transactions, newest first. A notice the company filed again is counted once.
dealings.sideOtherNote: Other: a gift, transfer, inheritance or wording that does not say purchase or disposal. Never counted as either.
dealings.flowsIntro: Disclosed purchases and disposals by directors and their related parties, per company, in the {window} to {date}. Companies are listed by the total value dealt in either direction, largest first.
dealings.clusterNote: Cluster: two or more different accounts made purchases in the window, and purchases exceeded disposals by value. It describes the disclosures; it is not a signal.
dealings.noFlows: No purchases or disposals were disclosed in this window.
dealings.more: {count} more companies with smaller dealings are not listed.
dealings.largeIntro: Dealings of Rs 10 mn or more in the 30 days to {date}.
dealings.noLarge: No dealings of Rs 10 mn or more in the 30 days to {date}.
dealings.ownGroupFlag: Same ownership group as the company
dealings.ownGroupNote: Same ownership group: the account that dealt is in the company's own ownership group (the company's parent, a company under the same parent, or the company itself), as worked out from the companies' top-20 shareholder lists.
dealings.previewNote: Free access shows the money flows a week late.

panel.title: Directors' dealings
panel.note: Disclosed by the company to the CSE; the company code covers all its share classes. Names are not shown.
panel.none: No dealings by this company's directors are in our records.

dealings.accountsIntro: Each account that disclosed dealings in the {window} to {date}, by the total value dealt in either direction. An account is a director, or a related party such as a family member or a company.

sections.recentSum: The latest {count} dealings disclosed; the most recent on {date}
sections.recentWhy: Listed companies must tell the CSE when their directors, or accounts related to them, trade the company's shares. Every investor can see what the people closest to a company did.
sections.recentHow: Each row is one transaction as the company filed it: the date of the dealing, purchase or disposal, the number of shares, the price and the value, the director and the account that dealt, and how many weekdays later it was disclosed. The notice link opens the company's own filing.
sections.flowsLocked: Which companies saw the most dealing by directors and related accounts, and in which direction
sections.flowsWhy: One dealing can have personal reasons. Several different directors or related accounts making purchases in the same company within a short time, or large values relative to the company, are easier to notice when the dealings are added up by company.
sections.flowsHow: Companies are listed by total value dealt (purchases plus disposals): activity, not direction. Net is purchases less disposals. A cluster marks a company where two or more different accounts made purchases and purchases exceeded disposals. The window tabs change the period; each ends on the latest dealing date.
sections.largeSum: {count} dealings of Rs 10 mn or more in the 30 days to {date}
sections.largeWhy: The largest single dealings are the ones most likely to matter to a company's share register and to its share price.
sections.largeHow: Each large dealing shows the director and the account, and marks accounts within the company's own ownership group: moves inside a group can be restructuring rather than a view on the shares.
sections.accountsSum: The {count} accounts with the largest value dealt
sections.accountsWhy: The same people and companies appear across several listed companies. Adding up their dealings shows who was most active across the market.
sections.accountsHow: Each account is named as filed, with the group it belongs to where known, the value it purchased and disposed of, and the companies it dealt in.

share.beta: Beta against the ASPI (as published by the CSE)
share.totalReturnSeries: Total return (dividends and share changes included)
share.chartNote: Both lines start at the close on {date}. The total-return line adds back the share's confirmed dividends and corrects for its sub-divisions, scrip dividends and rights issues, so it shows the value of the shares owned on the first day, with their dividends kept in the shares. The price line is the CSE's published price, which drops at each of those events.
share.totalReturnAsOf: Total return to {date}, the last session this share traded.
share.actionsNote: Read from the CSE's own announcement records. A figure awaiting confirmation was read from the announcement's text, or is incomplete; it is not used in the total return until it has been checked against the announcement.
share.noActions: No dividends or other corporate actions found in the CSE's records for this share since June 2025.

amounts.rightsNoPrice: {new} new for every {existing}, price to be confirmed

share.figuresNote: Read from the company's interim reports. A figure is shown only when it agrees with the profit or equity line in the same report; per-share figures use today's number of shares, so the P/E is market value ÷ profit over the last twelve months.
share.figuresNone: No figures that reconcile inside the company's reports yet.
share.divTtm: Rs {amount} of dividends per share in the last 12 months
share.ttmMissing: Not all of the last four quarters' profits are in the reports, so there is no 12-month figure.
share.votingPriceNote: Ratios use the voting share's price.
share.ownersNote: From the twenty largest shareholders listed in the company's report for the period to {date}. Percentages are of the voting shares.
share.ownersNone: No checked shareholder list for this company yet.

ownersStatus.no_text: The latest report is a scanned image without text, so its shareholder list cannot be read.
ownersStatus.no_table: No shareholder list was found in the latest report.
ownersStatus.download_failed: The latest report could not be downloaded yet.
ownersStatus.unverified: The shareholder list in the latest report did not pass the checks (its numbers do not agree with each other or with the CSE's share count), so it is not used.

share.controlled: {owner}, with {pct} of the votes: control (more than 50%)
share.influence: {owner}, with {pct} of the votes: influence (20% to 50%)
share.noControl: No single block has 20% or more of the votes.
share.groupNamed: {name}: {count, plural, one {this company only} other {# listed companies}}
share.groupUnnamed: Headed by {owner}: {count, plural, one {this company only} other {# listed companies}}
share.freeFloatNote: Voting shares not held by the company itself or by any block of 10% or more. Directors' smaller holdings cannot be told apart in the list, so the true figure is lower.
share.top20Note: As the company's report for the period to {date} lists them, with each holder named as resolved: shares held through a custodian or a margin account are credited to the owner, whose name as filed is shown beneath. The percentage is of the class's issued shares, as the report prints it.
share.leadLine: {symbol} on the Colombo Stock Exchange. Everything on this page comes from the CSE's own data and the company's filings.

glance.close: The price closed at {price} on {date}, {change} on the day.
glance.closeNoTrade: The share did not trade on {date}; its last close was {price}.
glance.rel3mMore: Over three months the price changed {ret}, {gap} percentage points more than the ASPI.
glance.rel3mLess: Over three months the price changed {ret}, {gap} percentage points less than the ASPI.
glance.tr3m: With dividends and share changes included, the three-month return was {tr}.
glance.figures: P/E {pe}, P/B {pb} and a dividend yield of {dy}, from the report for the period to {date}.
glance.figuresLoss: The company made a loss over the last twelve months; P/B {pb}, from the report for the period to {date}.
glance.owners: The 20 largest shareholders own {top20}; the largest is {name}, with {pct}.
glance.dealings: Directors reported {count, plural, one {# dealing} other {# dealings}} in the last year; the latest on {date}.
glance.dealingsNone: No directors' dealings were reported in the last year.

sections.priceSum: Price {ret3m} over three months; {tr3m} with dividends included
sections.priceWhy: The CSE's price drops when a dividend is paid or shares are split, so the price alone understates what shareholders received. The total-return line puts dividends and share changes back.
sections.priceHow: Both lines start at the same point. Where the total-return line is above the price line, dividends or share changes added to the return. The returns table compares the share with the ASPI over the same periods: a positive gap means the share's price did better than the market as a whole.
sections.figuresSum: P/E {pe} · P/B {pb} · Return on equity {roe} · Dividend yield {dy}
sections.figuresSumNone: Figures from the company's latest interim report
sections.figuresWhy: These relate the share price to what the company earns, what it owns and what it pays out, so companies of different sizes can be compared.
sections.figuresHow: Compare a figure with the same company's own past and with similar companies, not with a fixed rule. A low P/E can reflect low expected growth or a one-off profit; after a loss, the P/E has no meaning.
sections.ownersSum: The 20 largest shareholders own {top20}; free float about {ff}
sections.ownersSumNone: Shareholders from the company's latest interim report
sections.ownersWhy: Who owns a company affects how freely its shares trade and who has a say in it. A company within a group often moves with the group's decisions.
sections.ownersHow: Start with the largest block and the ownership group, then the free-float estimate: the part of the company likely to change hands. A small free float can mean thin trading and larger price swings.
sections.actionsSum: {count, plural, one {# action} other {# actions}} recorded; the latest ex-date {date}
sections.actionsWhy: Dividends, splits, scrip issues and rights issues change the share price without changing the value of what a shareholder owns. They explain the sudden steps in the price chart.
sections.actionsHow: The ex-date is the first day a purchase no longer carries the right to the dividend or issue; the price usually falls by about its value that day. A row awaiting confirmation is not used in the total return until it has been checked.
sections.dealingsSum: {count, plural, one {# dealing} other {# dealings}} on record; the latest on {date}
sections.dealingsWhy: Directors know their company well, so the CSE requires their dealings in its shares to be disclosed for every investor to see.
sections.dealingsHow: Look at the size of a dealing against the company's usual turnover, and at patterns across several directors. A single dealing can have personal reasons, such as tax, a loan or a family transfer, and is not a forecast.

bonds.title: Government bonds
bonds.intro: LKR treasury bonds: the dealers' daily quotes, a yield curve fitted to them, and how actively each bond trades.
bonds.curveNote: A Nelson-Siegel curve fitted to the dealers' average quotes, each weighted by how tight its bid-offer spread is. Trades are not used in the fit; they show where business was done.
bonds.fitStats: {n} quotes; fit error {rmse} bp. {trades, plural, =0 {No trades checked yet} one {Checked against # traded bond} other {Checked against # traded bonds}}.
bonds.tradeBias: Trades printed {bias} bp from the curve (median).
bonds.tableNote: Residual: the quoted mid minus the curve, in basis points. Positive means the bond's quoted yield is above the curve. “Wide”: the dealers' bid and offer are more than 50 bp apart, usually an administered quote, so it has little weight in the curve.
bonds.oneWay: one-way quote: not in the fit
bonds.tierHelp: Benchmark: auctioned in the last 120 days and traded on at least 8 of the last 60 days. Active: traded on at least 10 of the last 60 days. Less traded: quoted but traded less often.
bonds.leadLong: Sri Lanka's government bonds as the dealers quoted them today, the yield curve fitted through those quotes, and each bond measured against it. Bond yields are the base on which savings rates and share valuations rest.

glance.slopeUp: The curve slopes upward: the 10-year yield is {bp} bp above the 1-year.
glance.slopeDown: The curve slopes downward: the 10-year yield is {bp} bp below the 1-year.
glance.quoted: Dealers quoted {n} bonds; {trades, plural, =0 {no trades were reported} one {# trade was reported} other {# trades were reported}}.
glance.fit: The fitted curve sits on average {rmse} bp from the dealers' quotes.

sections.curveWhy: The curve shows what the government pays to borrow for each length of time. Every rupee interest rate, from treasury bills to fixed deposits, is set with it in view.
sections.curveHow: Each dot is a bond: across, the years it has left; up, its yield. The line is the smooth curve that fits them best. A dot above the line is quoted at a higher yield than bonds of a similar maturity, a dot below at a lower one. Hollow dots are quotes with a wide gap between bid and offer, which count for less in the fit.
sections.tableSum: {n} bonds quoted; distance from the curve, trading activity and turnover for each
sections.tableWhy: The table puts every bond's quote, its distance from the curve and how actively it trades side by side, so a figure can be read with its context.
sections.tableHow: Bonds are listed by maturity. The distance from the curve is in basis points (100 bp = 1%). A bond that rarely trades can sit far from the curve simply because its quote is seldom tested; the activity column shows which those are. Select a bond for its full page.
sections.furtherLead: Tools for following individual bonds closely. Each one is explained in a guide that anyone can read.

tools.zscores: How unusual each bond's distance from the curve is today, compared with its own recent history.
tools.execution: How far, typically, trades were done from the dealers' quoted yields over the last 20 days.
tools.carry: What each bond earns if rates do not move, and how its price reacts when they do.

bonds.guideBonds: Bonds and bills, step by step
bonds.searchPlaceholder: Bond name, ISIN or maturity year

bond.label: Series
bond.synthetic: No PDMO release names this bond with an ISIN; it is identified by its maturity and coupon.
bond.historyWindow: Free access shows the last 30 days; {tier} and above show the full history.
bond.zTitle: How unusual is its position today?
bond.zBody: Its distance from the curve, compared with its own last 60 days. 0 is typical; beyond ±2 is rare.
bond.tradesNone: No trades in this bond in the period shown.
bond.scenarioNote: Estimated from the bond's duration and convexity at today's yield; actual prices also depend on the curve's shape and on trading.

sections.bondWhy: A bond's yield is the yearly return built into today's price if it is kept until it matures. It is the number to compare with a fixed deposit or a treasury bill of a similar length.
sections.bondHow: The mid yield is halfway between the yield dealers quote to purchase the bond (bid) and to dispose of it (offer). A wide gap between the two means fewer dealers were ready to trade at close to one price. The chart shows how the mid yield moved over time.
sections.curveWhy: Comparing a bond with the fitted curve shows whether it is quoted in line with bonds of a similar maturity, or higher or lower than them.
sections.curveHow: Above zero, the bond yields more than the curve at its maturity; below zero, less. The distance often has ordinary reasons: how often the bond trades, its coupon, or a recent auction. It describes today's quote; it says nothing about tomorrow's.
sections.unusualLocked: Today's distance from the curve compared with this bond's own recent history
sections.unusualWhy: A bond can always sit a little above or below the curve. What is informative is a distance unusual for that particular bond, which the z-score measures.
sections.unusualHow: 0 means a typical day for this bond; +2 or −2 means a distance seen only rarely in its last 60 observations. It describes the bond's position against its own past; it is not a forecast of where the bond goes next.
sections.tradesWhy: Dealers' quotes show where they say they would deal; reported trades show where business was actually done.
sections.tradesHow: Each trade is shown with its distance from the curve on that day. Trades close to the quotes confirm them; trades far away suggest the screen was not where business would happen.
sections.carrySum: Duration {d} · carry and roll-down {total} bp a year
sections.carryLocked: What the bond earns if rates do not move, and how its price reacts when they do
sections.carryWhy: Carry and roll-down estimate what a bond earns, per year, if the curve stays where it is. Duration and convexity show how much its price changes when yields move.
sections.carryHow: Carry is the bond's yield less the cost of funding it (here, the 12-month treasury bill yield plus a small margin); roll-down is the gain as the bond ages and slides along an upward-sloping curve, measured over a quarter and stated per year. A duration of 5 means a 1% rise in yields lowers the price by about 5%. The scenario table applies those figures to yield moves of different sizes.

zscores.title: Unusual positions against the curve
zscores.intro: Each bond's distance from the curve, compared with that bond's own previous 60 observations. A z-score of +2 means the residual is two standard deviations above its own recent average. This describes the data; it is not a forecast.
zscores.pairsNote: The residual spread between this bond and each bond of similar maturity (or, for two auctioned bonds, any maturity), against its own history. Choose another bond in the table above.
zscores.pairsNone: No pair with enough common history on this date.
zscores.why: Every bond sits a little above or below the fitted curve for ordinary reasons. This page shows which bonds are, today, unusually far from their own normal distance, and the same for the gap between neighbouring bonds.
zscores.how: Bonds are listed by maturity, never ranked. For each: its distance from the curve today, how far that is from its own recent average, the usual size of its daily variation (standard deviation), and the ratio of the two (the z-score). Around 0 is ordinary; beyond +2 or −2 is rare for that bond. Choose a bond to see its pairs with neighbouring bonds. Nothing here forecasts where a bond goes next.

execution.title: Trades against quotes
execution.intro: Where executed trades printed relative to the dealers' quoted mid, as a 20-day median. Positive: trades at higher yields (lower prices) than the quotes.
execution.why: Dealers' screens show where they say they would deal; trades show where business was done. The gap between the two tells you how far a quoted yield can be relied on.
execution.how: One figure for the whole market: the median gap, over the last 20 calendar days, between the yield at which bonds traded and their quoted mid on the same day, counting every bond that both quoted and traded. Positive means trades were done at higher yields (lower prices) than the screen showed; negative, at lower yields. It is reported only when there are at least 8 such bond-days, and it describes the recent past, not a precise level.

carry.title: Carry, rolldown and duration
carry.intro: What each bond's yield earns over a stated funding rate, plus rolldown along an unchanged curve, per year and per year of duration. The funding rate is the 12-month treasury bill plus 5 bp; your own funding cost will differ.
carry.why: Two bonds with the same yield can earn different amounts over time, depending on the cost of funding them and how they age along the curve. Per unit of duration, bonds of different lengths become comparable.
carry.how: All figures are in basis points per year. Carry: the bond's yield less the funding rate. Roll-down: the gain as the bond ages along an unchanged curve. Their total divided by duration puts long and short bonds on the same footing. These are estimates under an unchanged curve; when yields move, duration says how much the price changes.

methods.title: Methods
methods.intro: Every number on this site comes from one of these models. Each page states the method, its assumptions and its limits, and how it was checked.

about.title: About
about.whatBody: We collect the market's public data each day, apply stated methods to it, and show the result with an explanation of what it means and how to read it. ZinvestIQ offers information, tools and education only: it never says what to do with anyone's money.
about.sourcesBody: Share prices, indices and market statistics: Colombo Stock Exchange. Government bond quotes, trades, volumes and auctions: Public Debt Management Office, Ministry of Finance. Interest rates and treasury bill yields: Central Bank of Sri Lanka. Consumer prices: Department of Census and Statistics, Sri Lanka. Data is used only where the source's terms allow it.
about.tiersBody: Most of the site is free. Some analysis will be part of paid tiers (Plus, Pro, Professional) once accounts open. The tier rules are applied on our server: information outside your tier is never sent to your browser.
about.correctionsBody: Sources are stored exactly as published, and every calculation is versioned. When a source corrects a figure, the correction is applied and the earlier value is kept on record.
about.lead: ZinvestIQ explains Sri Lanka's markets in plain language: the share market, government bonds and treasury bills, and savings rates, side by side, from public sources, with every method published.
about.differBody: Three rules shape everything on the site. Explained, not rated: no signals, scores, stances or forecasts, anywhere. Numbers you can check: every figure comes from a published method with a version number, computed wherever possible from the data available on that day, and earlier values are kept on record when a source revises something. The whole picture: shares, government securities and savings are read together, because interest rates connect them.

learn.title: Learn
learn.intro: Plain-language guides to Sri Lanka's markets, from the basics to the tools bond professionals use. Every guide is free to read, and each links to the part of the site it explains.

aspi.name: ASPI (All Share Price Index)
aspi.short: The CSE's broadest index: the combined price of every listed company's shares.
aspi.long: The All Share Price Index adds up the market value of every company listed on the Colombo Stock Exchange and compares it with a base value. When most large companies' share prices rise, the ASPI rises. It measures prices only; the ASPI total return index also counts dividends.

spsl20.name: S&P SL20
spsl20.short: An index of 20 of the CSE's largest and most traded companies.
spsl20.long: Calculated with S&P Dow Jones Indices, the S&P SL20 follows 20 large, frequently traded companies, so it shows how the market's biggest names moved, separately from the many small ones in the ASPI.

turnover.name: Turnover
turnover.short: The rupee value of all shares that changed hands in a session.
turnover.long: Turnover is the total value of the day's trades. High turnover means many investors were active; the site also compares it with the average of the last 20 sessions.

breadth.name: Market breadth
breadth.short: How many shares rose, fell or did not change.
breadth.long: Breadth shows whether a move was shared by most companies or driven by a few. An index can rise while more shares fall than rise, if a few large companies move up.

foreign.name: Foreign purchases and sales
foreign.short: Trades by investors based outside Sri Lanka, as the CSE reports them.
foreign.long: The CSE publishes the value of shares foreign investors purchased and disposed of each day. The difference is their net flow for the day.

pe.name: Price / earnings (P/E)
pe.short: Share price divided by the company's profit per share over the last year.
pe.long: A P/E of 10 means the price equals ten years of the company's current yearly profit. Comparing P/Es only makes sense between similar companies, and profits change over time.

pbv.name: Price / book (P/B, P/BV)
pbv.short: Share price compared with the company's net assets per share.
pbv.long: Book value is what the company owns minus what it owes, per share, as shown in its accounts. A P/BV of 1 means the market price equals that accounting value.

dividendYield.name: Dividend yield
dividendYield.short: Dividends paid over the last year as a percentage of the share price.
dividendYield.long: If a share costs Rs 100 and paid Rs 5 in dividends over the last year, its dividend yield is 5%. Past dividends are not a promise of future ones.

marketCap.name: Market capitalisation
marketCap.short: The value of all of a company's shares at today's price.
marketCap.long: Shares in issue multiplied by the share price. It shows a company's size as the market values it today.

range52.name: 52-week range
range52.short: The lowest and highest prices of the past year, and where today's price sits between them.
range52.long: 0% means today's price is at the year's low and 100% at its high. The CSE publishes these prices unadjusted, so a split or bonus issue can distort them.

relative.name: Return against the ASPI
relative.short: A share's price change minus the index's over the same period.
relative.long: Positive means the share's price moved up more, or down less, than the market as a whole over that period; negative means the opposite.

beta.name: Beta
beta.short: How much a share has tended to move when the market moves.
beta.long: A beta of 1 means it has moved roughly in step with the market, above 1 by more, below 1 by less. It is measured on past prices (here as the CSE publishes it) and changes over time.

yield.name: Yield
yield.short: The yearly return built into a bond's price today, if it is kept until it matures.
yield.long: A bond pays fixed coupons and repays its face value at maturity. When its price falls, the same payments are a larger return on the price, so the yield rises: price and yield always move in opposite directions.

bp.name: Basis point (bp)
bp.short: One hundredth of a percentage point: 0.25% is 25 bp.
bp.long: Bond yields move in small steps, so they are measured in basis points. A yield rising from 11.00% to 11.25% has risen by 25 bp.

curve.name: Yield curve
curve.short: Government bond yields lined up by how many years each bond has left.
curve.long: The curve shows what the government pays to borrow for different lengths of time. It usually slopes upward, because lenders expect more for lending longer. We fit a smooth Nelson-Siegel curve through the dealers' quotes each day.

residual.name: Distance from the curve
residual.short: How far a bond's quoted yield sits above (+) or below (−) the fitted curve, in bp.
residual.long: A bond far from the curve is quoted differently from bonds of similar maturity. Reasons include how often it trades, its coupon and recent auctions; it is a description, not a forecast.

zscore.name: Z-score
zscore.short: How unusual today's value is compared with its own recent history.
zscore.long: A z-score of 0 means a typical day; +2 or −2 means a value seen only rarely in the last 60 observations. It says nothing about what happens next.

liquidity.name: Trading activity
liquidity.short: How often and how much a bond trades: benchmark, active or less traded.
liquidity.long: A bond that trades often has firmer prices. Less traded bonds' quotes can sit further from where business would actually be done.

bidOffer.name: Bid and offer
bidOffer.short: The yields dealers quote for purchasing (bid) and for disposing of (offer) a bond.
bidOffer.long: The mid is halfway between them. A wide gap between bid and offer means the quote is less firm.

duration.name: Duration
duration.short: How sensitive a bond's price is to a change in yields.
duration.long: With a duration of 4, a 1 percentage point rise in yield lowers the price by about 4%, and a fall raises it by about 4%. Longer bonds have longer durations.

convexity.name: Convexity
convexity.short: The bend in the price–yield relationship.
convexity.long: Because of convexity, a bond's price rises a little more when yields fall than it drops when yields rise by the same amount. It matters most for large moves and long bonds.

carry.name: Carry
carry.short: What a bond's yield earns above a stated funding rate, per year.
carry.long: Here the funding rate is the 12-month treasury bill plus 5 bp. Your own costs will differ, so carry is a reference point, not a return you would get.

rolldown.name: Rolldown
rolldown.short: The price change from a bond getting shorter along an unchanged curve.
rolldown.long: As time passes a bond's remaining life shortens; on an upward-sloping curve its yield then moves toward the lower yields of shorter bonds, which raises its price, if the curve stays the same.

methodVersion.name: Method version
methodVersion.short: Every calculation has a version number.
methodVersion.long: When we change how something is calculated, the version changes and the earlier version stays on record, so a figure can always be traced to the method that produced it.

fixedDeposit.name: Fixed deposit
fixedDeposit.short: Money placed with a bank or finance company for a fixed term, at an interest rate agreed at the start.
fixedDeposit.long: The interest is paid at the end of the term (or monthly, at a slightly lower rate), and the money cannot usually be withdrawn early without losing some interest. Deposits at licensed banks and finance companies are insured up to Rs 1,100,000 per depositor at each institution.

treasuryBill.name: Treasury bill
treasuryBill.short: A short-term loan to the Government of Sri Lanka, for 91, 182 or 364 days.
treasuryBill.long: A bill pays no coupon: it is issued below its face value and repaid at face value, and the difference is the interest. The yield is set at the weekly auctions run by the Public Debt Management Office. Since April 2018 nothing is deducted from bill interest; it is taxed at each person's own income tax rate.

inflation.name: Inflation
inflation.short: How fast prices rise, usually measured over the last 12 months.
inflation.long: In Sri Lanka the headline measure is the Colombo Consumer Price Index (CCPI), published monthly by the Department of Census and Statistics. When prices rise 10% in a year, Rs 110 at the end pays for what Rs 100 paid for at the start.

realReturn.name: Real return
realReturn.short: Growth after inflation: what the money is worth in the prices of the day it was saved.
realReturn.long: A deposit that earns 10% in a year when prices rise 6% has grown by about 4% in real terms. When inflation is higher than the interest rate, the real return is negative: the money pays for less at the end than at the start, even though there are more rupees.

awfdr.name: AWFDR and AWNFDR
awfdr.short: Average fixed deposit rates the Central Bank computes each month across licensed commercial banks.
awfdr.long: The AWFDR (average weighted fixed deposit rate) averages the rates on all fixed deposits that banks have taken, including those placed years ago. The AWNFDR (average weighted new fixed deposit rate, published from April 2014) averages only the deposits taken during the month, so it follows current rates more closely. Both cover all terms, not only 12 months, and neither is the rate of any one bank.

exDate.name: Ex-date
exDate.short: The first session in which a share trades without its next dividend or other entitlement.
exDate.long: Someone who acquires the share on or after the ex-date does not receive that dividend, new shares or rights; the seller does. The price usually drops on the ex-date by about the value of what was paid out, which is not a loss for the shareholder, because they keep the dividend or the new shares.

totalReturn.name: Total return
totalReturn.short: The price change plus dividends, with splits, scrip and rights issues taken into account.
totalReturn.long: A share's published price falls when it pays a dividend or splits, even though its owners lose nothing. The total return adds the dividends back and corrects for changes in the number of shares, so it measures what the shares owned at the start would be worth with their dividends kept in the shares. Past returns do not predict future ones.

directorsDealings.name: Directors' dealings
directorsDealings.short: A director's purchase or disposal of shares in their own company, which the company must disclose to the stock exchange.
directorsDealings.long: The CSE's listing rules require a listed company to announce, within a few market days, every dealing in its shares by its directors, in their own name or through a related party. The notice gives the director's role, the account, and each transaction's date, number of shares and price. Directors deal for many reasons, such as personal finances, taxes, estates or share schemes, so one dealing on its own says little.

relatedParty.name: Related party
relatedParty.short: A person or company connected with a director, such as a close relative or a company the director controls or sits on the board of.
relatedParty.long: A director must disclose dealings through these accounts as well as in their own name. The notice names the related account; we show only that the dealing was through a related party.

cluster.name: Cluster
cluster.short: Two or more different accounts making purchases of the same company's shares within one window, with purchases exceeding disposals by value.
cluster.long: We mark a cluster when, within the window, at least two distinct directors or related parties made purchases and the value of purchases was larger than the value of disposals. It describes what was disclosed. It is not a signal and says nothing about where the price will go.

eps.name: Earnings per share (EPS)
eps.short: The company's profit divided by its number of shares.
eps.long: Here it is the profit attributable to the company's shareholders over the last four quarters, divided by today's number of shares. It is shown only when all four quarters' profits are in the company's reports.

navPerShare.name: Net assets per share
navPerShare.short: What the company owns minus what it owes, per share, as shown in its accounts.
navPerShare.long: Also called book value per share. Here it is the equity attributable to the company's shareholders in its latest report, divided by today's number of shares.

roe.name: Return on equity (ROE)
roe.short: Profit over the last year as a percentage of the shareholders' equity.
roe.long: An ROE of 15% means the company earned Rs 15 over the last year for every Rs 100 of net assets in its accounts. It is EPS over the last 12 months divided by net assets per share.

freeFloat.name: Free float
freeFloat.short: The share of a company's shares that is not held by its controlling or large holders.
freeFloat.long: Shares held by a parent company, the company itself or any holder with 10% or more are not part of the free float. Here it is estimated from the twenty largest shareholders the company lists; directors' smaller holdings cannot be told apart, so the true free float is lower.

ownershipGroup.name: Ownership group
ownershipGroup.short: Listed companies that answer to the same owner.
ownershipGroup.long: Found by following each company's largest voting block (20% or more) upward until an owner that is not itself a listed company. Funds, the state and nominee accounts never head a group.

markets-map.title: How Sri Lanka's markets fit together
markets-map.summary: Shares, government bonds and bills, and fixed deposits are priced against each other. Interest rates are the thread that connects them.
keypoints: A rupee can be lent to a bank (a fixed deposit), lent to the government (a treasury bill or bond) or used to own part of a company (a share).
The government's borrowing rates, the yield curve, are the base: the return on the safest rupee investment for each length of time.
Fixed-deposit rates move with treasury bill yields, usually with a lag.
Shares are uncertain, so they are judged against what a government bill pays for certain.
What matters in the end is the return left after tax and inflation.

p: A Sri Lankan saver has three main choices. A fixed deposit lends money to a bank or finance company for a set time at a set rate. A treasury bill or bond lends it to the government. A share makes the investor a part-owner of a listed company, with a claim on its future profits and dividends.

They differ in what is promised. A deposit and a government security promise a stated rupee return if they are kept to the end. A share promises nothing: its dividends and its price depend on how the company does and on what other investors will pay.

The government borrows by issuing treasury bills (up to a year) and treasury bonds (two to twenty years or more) at regular auctions. The yields at those auctions, and in the trading that follows, are the return on lending to the government for each length of time. Lined up by maturity, they form the yield curve.

Because the government can raise taxes and issue rupees, its rupee borrowing is treated as the lowest-risk rupee investment. Its yields are the base that other rates are built on, and they follow the Central Bank's policy rate, inflation and the government's own borrowing needs.

Banks compete with the government for savers' money. When treasury bill yields rise, banks usually raise deposit rates, and when bill yields fall, deposit rates follow them down, typically with a delay of weeks or months.

For a saver, the headline rate is only the start. Tax is deducted from interest, and inflation reduces what the money can purchase. The real return, what is left after both, is what the savings comparison on this site measures.

A share's return is uncertain, so investors compare it with the certain return on a government bill. When bill yields are high, a share's dividends and expected growth have to offer more to attract money; when yields fall, the comparison changes in shares' favour.
This is why the share market often reacts to interest-rate news, and why the market's dividend yield and P/E are worth reading next to the yield curve.

The home page shows the day's share market and yield curve side by side. The bonds pages show every government bond against the curve. The savings page compares fixed deposits, bills and inflation since 2003. The share pages show each company's return with dividends included, its figures and its owners. The guides explain each step.

limits: The links between rates and prices apply on average and over time, not every day or for every company.
Other things move markets too: company results, politics, the exchange rate and foreign investors' decisions.
This guide explains how the markets relate; it does not say which is the better place for anyone's money.

shares-basics.title: Shares, step by step
shares-basics.summary: What a share is, what moves its price, what the indices measure, and how to read a share's page on this site.
keypoints: A share is part-ownership of a company: a claim on its profits, paid out as dividends or kept to grow the business.
Prices on the CSE move with what investors will pay, which reflects company results, interest rates and sentiment.
The ASPI measures the whole market; the S&P SL20 its 20 largest, most traded companies.
A share's page here goes from the latest price, to its return with dividends, to its figures, owners and directors' dealings.

p: When a company lists on the Colombo Stock Exchange, its shares can be traded between investors. Each share is a small piece of ownership. Shareholders vote at general meetings and receive the dividends the board declares.
Investing on the CSE needs an account with the Central Depository System (CDS), opened through a licensed stockbroker. The shares are held electronically in that account.

The price is simply the level at which the last trade was done. Over time it follows what investors expect the company to earn and pay out, and how they value those earnings against other choices, above all the yield on government securities.
Day to day, prices also move with news, with large investors' decisions and with the general mood of the market. On days with little trading, a few orders can move a price a long way.

The All Share Price Index (ASPI) combines the market value of every listed company, so the largest companies count for the most. The S&P Sri Lanka 20 follows 20 large, frequently traded companies. Sector indices group companies by industry.
An index can rise while most shares fall, if a few large companies go up. Market breadth, the count of shares that rose, fell or did not change, shows whether a move was widely shared.
At the top: the latest price and its change, where it sits in the past year's range, and the company's size (market capitalisation). Below it, 'At a glance' sums up the page in a few sentences.

Price and returns shows the price and the total return, which puts dividends and share changes back in, and compares the share with the ASPI over one week, one month and three months. Company figures relate the price to the company's profits, net assets and dividends. Who owns it lists the largest shareholders and estimates the free float. Dividends and other corporate actions list what the company paid and issued. Directors' dealings shows what its directors traded.
Each section opens with why it matters and how to read it, and links to the guide that explains it in full.

limits: Past prices and returns describe what happened; they do not predict what comes next.
Company figures come from interim reports that are a few months old by the time the next one appears.
Nothing on a share's page is a view on whether it suits any particular investor.

total-return.title: Price return and total return
total-return.summary: Why a share's price chart understates what its shareholders received, and how dividends, splits and rights issues are put back.
keypoints: On the ex-date of a dividend, the share price usually falls by about the dividend: shareholders have not lost anything.
Splits, scrip dividends and rights issues change the number of shares and the price without changing the value owned.
The total return puts those back, as if dividends had been kept in the shares.
Comparing companies, or a share with a fixed deposit, needs total return, not price return.

p: Suppose a share trades at Rs 100 and the company pays a dividend of Rs 5. From the ex-date, a purchase no longer carries the right to that dividend, so the price typically opens about Rs 5 lower. The price chart shows a fall of 5%, yet a shareholder has Rs 95 in shares and Rs 5 in cash: nothing was lost.
Over years, these steps add up. For a company that pays generous dividends, the price chart can look flat while shareholders did well.

A sub-division splits each share into several, at a proportionally lower price. A scrip dividend pays the dividend in new shares instead of cash. A rights issue lets existing shareholders take up new shares, usually at a discount. All of these change the price per share, so an unadjusted chart shows jumps that are not gains or losses.

sections.h: How the total return is built
p: ZinvestIQ starts from the CSE's published closing prices and each confirmed corporate action. On each ex-date it adjusts for the dividend or the change in the number of shares, so the total-return line shows the value of the shares owned at the start, with each dividend kept in the shares. Dividends are counted before withholding tax.
Corporate actions are read from the companies' announcements and checked; an action still awaiting confirmation is listed on the share's page but not used until it has been checked.

On a share's page, both lines start at the same point. Where the total-return line runs above the price line, dividends and share changes added to the return. The gap between them is the part of the return the price chart leaves out.

limits: Tax on dividends is not deducted, so the after-tax return is somewhat lower.
It assumes dividends were kept in the shares at the ex-date price; a shareholder who spent them has a different result.
A corporate action announced in an unusual way may take time to confirm, and the total return waits for it.

company-figures.title: Reading company figures
company-figures.summary: P/E, P/B, return on equity, earnings per share and dividend yield: what each measures, how they are computed here, and what they leave out.
keypoints: Each figure relates the share price to something in the company's accounts: profits, net assets or dividends.
They come from the company's latest interim reports, using the last twelve months.
Compare a figure with the company's own past and with similar companies, not with a fixed number.
A single figure never tells the whole story: a low P/E can have many reasons.

p: Earnings per share (EPS) is the profit attributable to shareholders over the last twelve months, divided by the number of shares. The price-to-earnings ratio (P/E) divides the share price by EPS. A P/E of 10 means the price equals ten years of the company's current yearly profit.

A low P/E can reflect low expected growth, a risky business, or a one-off profit that inflated EPS. A high P/E can reflect high expected growth or a temporary dip in profits. When a company makes a loss, the P/E has no meaning and is not shown.

sections.h: Net assets per share and P/B
p: Net assets per share (book value) is what the company owns less what it owes, per share, as its accounts state it. Price-to-book (P/B) divides the share price by it. A P/B of 1 means the market values the company at its accounting value.
P/B is most informative for companies whose assets are mostly financial, such as banks and finance companies, and least for companies whose value lies in brands or people.

Return on equity (ROE) divides the last twelve months' profit by net assets: how much profit the company made on the shareholders' money it uses. Read together, P/B and ROE explain each other: a company that earns a high return on its equity usually trades at a higher P/B.

The dividend yield is the dividends paid over the last twelve months as a percentage of today's price. It is worth comparing with fixed-deposit rates and treasury bill yields, remembering that dividends are not promised and can be cut.

ZinvestIQ reads each company's interim reports as filed with the CSE, adds up the last four quarters, and shows a figure only when it agrees with the profit or equity line in the same report. Per-share figures use today's number of shares, and each figure links to the report it came from.

limits: Accounts are backward-looking and a few months old by the time they are published.
One-off gains or losses can distort a year's profit and every figure built on it.
Figures say nothing on their own about whether a price is high or low for a particular investor's purposes.

ownership.title: Who owns a company, and why it matters
ownership.summary: Reading the largest shareholders, control, ownership groups and the free float from the companies' own reports.
keypoints: Listed companies publish their 20 largest shareholders in each interim report.
A single block above 50% controls a company; 20% to 50% gives influence.
Many Sri Lankan companies belong to groups: a parent controls several listed companies.
The free float, the part likely to change hands, affects how easily the shares trade.

p: Each quarter, a listed company publishes its 20 largest shareholders with their holdings. ZinvestIQ reads those lists, resolves holdings through custodian and margin accounts to the owner where the filing shows it, and groups the owners by type: listed companies, other companies, funds, insurers and the state, and individuals.

Votes are added up by block: a holder's own accounts plus the companies it controls. A block of more than 50% of the voting shares controls the company; one of 20% to 50% has influence over it. A controlled company's decisions, on dividends, on new shares and on strategy, are in practice its controller's.

Many listed companies are part of a group: a holding company controls several others, which may in turn control more. ZinvestIQ follows these chains and names each company's group, with the other listed companies in it, so the reader can see when several shares belong to one family of businesses.

The free float estimates the part of a company's voting shares not held by the company itself, by companies it controls, or by blocks of 10% or more. A small free float can mean thin trading, wider gaps between purchase and sale prices, and larger price moves on small orders.

limits: The lists are as at the report date and change in between.
Holdings below the top 20, including many directors' holdings, are not visible, so the free float is an estimate.
Who owns a company describes its register; it is not a view on the shares.

directors-dealings.title: Directors' dealings, explained
directors-dealings.summary: What listed companies must disclose about their directors' trading, how to read a dealing, and what it can and cannot tell you.
keypoints: Directors and accounts related to them must disclose dealings in their company's shares to the CSE.
Each dealing shows who, which account, purchase or disposal, how many shares, at what price, and when it was disclosed.
Patterns, several directors dealing within a short time, are more informative than a single dealing.
A dealing can have personal reasons and is never a forecast.

p: Directors know their company better than outside investors. To keep the market fair, the CSE's rules require a listed company to announce its directors' dealings in its shares, including dealings by accounts related to them, promptly after they happen. The notices are public.

ZinvestIQ reads each notice and records the date of the dealing, whether it was a purchase or a disposal, the number of shares, the price and the value, the director, the account that dealt as filed, and how many weekdays passed before it was disclosed. Every row links to the company's own notice.

Related accounts are companies or family members linked to the director. A dealing by a company in the same ownership group can be a transfer within the group rather than a view on the shares; the site marks those.

The size of a dealing compared with the company's usual daily turnover and with the director's position. Whether several directors dealt in the same direction within a few weeks. Whether purchases came after a fall in the price, or disposals after a rise. And how long the disclosure took.

limits: A dealing can be for tax, a loan, an inheritance or a family transfer, with no connection to the company's prospects.
Directors' smaller holdings and dealings through accounts not disclosed as related are not visible.
Past dealings say nothing certain about future prices.

bonds-basics.title: Bonds and bills, step by step
bonds-basics.summary: How treasury bills and bonds work, why a bond's price and its yield move in opposite directions, and how they compare with a fixed deposit.
keypoints: Treasury bills last up to a year and pay no coupon: they are issued below face value and repaid in full.
Treasury bonds pay a fixed coupon twice a year and repay their face value at maturity, two to twenty years or more ahead.
A bond's yield is the yearly return built into today's price if it is kept until it matures.
When yields rise, existing bonds' prices fall, and the other way round.

p: The government issues treasury bills of about three, six and twelve months. A bill pays no interest along the way: it is issued at a discount and repaid at its full face value. The difference is the return. A Rs 100,000 one-year bill issued at Rs 90,000 pays a yield of about 11%.

Treasury bonds lend to the government for longer. Each pays a fixed coupon every six months, stated as a yearly percentage of its face value, and repays the face value at maturity. After they are issued at auction, bonds are traded between investors through primary dealers and banks, which publish the yields at which they would deal.

A bond's coupons are fixed, but its price changes. If market yields rise after a bond was issued, new bonds pay more, so the older bond's price falls until its yield matches. If yields fall, the older bond's price rises. Price and yield always move in opposite directions.

The longer the bond, the more its price moves for the same change in yield. That matters only if the bond is disposed of before maturity: kept to the end, it repays its face value whatever happened in between.

A bill or bond and a fixed deposit both pay a known rupee return if kept to the end. The differences are the borrower (the government or a bank), whether the money can be reached before the end and at what price, and the tax treatment. Comparing the yield on a bond with the rate on a deposit of the same length is the starting point; the savings page shows how the two compared since 2003.

The bonds page lists every government bond the dealers quoted today, with its yield, its distance from the fitted curve and how actively it trades. Each bond's own page shows its yield over time and, in the paid plans, how unusual its position is and what it earns.

limits: Government securities are the lowest-risk rupee investment, but their value before maturity moves with yields.
Quoted yields are dealers' screens; the yield actually obtained depends on the dealer and the amount.
Inflation can still leave a fixed return worth less in real terms.

yield-curve.title: The yield curve, and how to read it
yield-curve.summary: What the yield curve shows, why it usually slopes upward, what moves it, and how ZinvestIQ fits it each day.
keypoints: The yield curve lines up government yields by how long each bond or bill has left.
It usually slopes upward: lending for longer usually earns more.
It moves with the Central Bank's policy rate, inflation expectations and the government's borrowing.
ZinvestIQ fits one smooth curve through the dealers' quotes each day, and measures every bond against it.

p: Plot each government bond's yield against the years it has left and a pattern appears: the yield curve. It answers a simple question for every length of time: what does the government pay to borrow for that long? It is the base from which other rupee interest rates are set.

Normally the curve slopes upward: lenders want more for tying up money longer and for the risk that inflation or rates rise in the meantime. A flat curve means short and long yields are close. An inverted curve, with short yields above long ones, usually appears when short-term rates are high and expected to fall.

The short end follows the Central Bank's policy rate closely. The long end reflects expectations about inflation and future rates, and the amount the government needs to borrow. Auctions, the government's financing plans and changes in inflation all move parts of the curve.

Each day, ZinvestIQ takes the dealers' quoted yields for every government bond and fits a smooth Nelson-Siegel curve through them, giving less weight to quotes with a wide gap between bid and offer. On the chart, dots are bonds and the line is the fitted curve. A bond's distance from the line, in basis points, shows whether it is quoted higher or lower than bonds of a similar maturity.

limits: The curve is fitted to quotes, which can differ from where trades are done.
A smooth curve cannot follow every bond: some sit off it for ordinary reasons such as trading activity or coupon.
The curve's shape describes today's market; it does not forecast rates.

bond-relative-value.title: Why some bonds sit off the curve
bond-relative-value.summary: The ordinary reasons a bond is quoted above or below the fitted curve, and how a z-score says whether today's distance is unusual for that bond.
keypoints: A bond's distance from the curve (its residual) is measured in basis points: 100 bp = 1%.
Most distances have ordinary causes: how often the bond trades, its coupon, recent auctions.
What is informative is a distance unusual for that particular bond; the z-score measures it against the bond's own last 60 observations.
Pairs compare neighbouring bonds in the same way.

p: A smooth curve cannot pass through every bond. A bond that rarely trades may keep a stale quote. A bond just reopened at auction can sit higher while the new supply is absorbed. A bond with a much higher or lower coupon than its neighbours can be quoted differently because investors value income and price gains differently. Benchmark bonds that trade every day often sit slightly below the curve because they are easy to trade.
So a bond 20 bp above the curve is not, on its own, remarkable. What matters is whether 20 bp is unusual for that bond.

For each bond, ZinvestIQ takes its distance from the curve over its previous 60 observations, works out the average and the usual size of the day-to-day variation (the standard deviation), and compares today's distance with them: z = (today − average) ÷ standard deviation. The day being scored is never part of its own history.

A z-score near 0 is an ordinary day for that bond. Beyond +2 or −2, the distance is one seen only rarely in its recent history. The page also shows the deviation in basis points, because a large z on a bond that barely moves can be a small distance.

Neighbouring bonds usually move together. The gap between two of them, scored the same way, shows when one has moved away from the other more than usual. Choosing a bond on the page lists its pairs with the bonds around it.

Bonds are listed by maturity and never ranked, because the page describes each bond rather than picking any out. Read the z-score with the bond's trading activity: a high reading on a bond that rarely trades may only mean its quote has not been tested.

limits: Sixty observations is a short history from one market period; the past range may not be the right yardstick.
An unusual reading describes the past and is not a forecast of the bond's next move.
Quotes can differ from where business is done; see the guide on trades and quotes.

trades-vs-quotes.title: Dealer quotes and actual trades
trades-vs-quotes.summary: The difference between the yields dealers show on their screens and the yields at which bonds actually trade, and how ZinvestIQ measures it.
keypoints: Dealers publish the yields at which they would purchase (bid) and dispose of (offer) each bond: the quote screen.
Trades are reported separately, a day or more later.
The execution gap is the typical difference between trade yields and quoted mids over the last 20 days, across the market.
A positive gap means trades were done at higher yields, that is lower prices, than the screen showed.

p: Each day the Public Debt Management Office publishes the yields dealers quote for every government bond, and separately the trades reported in the secondary market. Quotes show where dealers say they would deal; trades show where business was done, in what amount.

On each day a bond both quoted and traded, its traded yield can be compared with its quoted mid. ZinvestIQ takes the median of those differences, in basis points, across every such bond-day in the last 20 calendar days. It is one figure for the market, published only when there are at least eight observations. A blended figure was chosen because, tested on past data, it described the next period better than figures split by maturity.

Every quote-based number, the curve itself included, inherits the gap. When trades are consistently done at yields above the screen, the screen overstates prices. The curve page shows trades as separate points for the same reason.

limits: A 20-day median of a few dozen observations moves with the market; it describes a recent period, not a precise level.
Trade reports arrive later than quotes, so the latest days are revised when they come in.
The gap for any one trade, or any one investor, can be very different.

money-flows.title: Money flows, explained
money-flows.summary: How directors' and related accounts' dealings are added up by company and by account, what a cluster is, and how to read the totals.
keypoints: Money flows add up the disclosed dealings of directors and their related accounts, by company and by account.
Companies are listed by total value dealt: activity, not direction.
A cluster is two or more different accounts making purchases in a company, with purchases exceeding disposals.
Free visitors see the flows a week after the dealings; Plus shows them on the day.

p: Each directors' dealing is one transaction. Money flows add them up over a window of 30, 90 or 365 days ending on the latest dealing date: for each company, the value purchased and disposed of, the net, how many different accounts made purchases or disposals, and how many dealings there were.

One director's purchase can have many reasons. Two or more different accounts making purchases in the same company within the window, with purchases above disposals, is a pattern worth noticing; the site marks it as a cluster.

Dealings of Rs 10 million or more in the last 30 days are listed separately, with the director and the account, and with a mark when the account belongs to the company's own ownership group, where the dealing may be a transfer within the group. The accounts table adds up each account's dealings across every company it dealt in.

limits: Only disclosed dealings by directors and related accounts are counted, not other investors' trading.
Large totals can come from a single transfer between related parties.
Flows describe past activity; they are not a forecast.

diversification.title: Diversification and risk
diversification.summary: Why a portfolio of many shares moves less than a single share, why some risk cannot be spread away, and why the number of shares matters on a small market such as the CSE.
keypoints: A single company can fall sharply for reasons of its own; a portfolio spreads that risk.
Shares that move differently from each other reduce a portfolio's ups and downs the most.
The market's own movements cannot be spread away: all shares are exposed to them.
On the CSE, a few large companies and sectors dominate, which limits how widely money can be spread.

p: A share's price moves for two kinds of reason. Some are its own: a contract won or lost, a fraud, a change of management. Others are shared by the whole market: interest rates, the economy, the exchange rate. Holdings across many companies average out the first kind, because one company's bad news is offset by another's good news. The second kind remains however many shares a portfolio contains.

Studies of large markets found that most of the reduction in a portfolio's ups and downs comes from the first dozen or two shares, with less from each one added after that (Evans and Archer, 1968); later work argued that more are needed for the benefit to be complete (Statman, 1987). The answer depends on how differently the shares move from each other.

On the CSE, a few large companies make up much of the market's value, and shares in the same sector or group often move together. Ten shares from one group or one sector spread risk far less than ten from different parts of the economy.

Volatility, the usual size of a portfolio's ups and downs, and the correlation between shares, how far they move together, are the standard measures. Each share's page shows its beta against the ASPI, a measure of how much it has tended to move with the market.

limits: Measures of risk are based on the past, and correlations tend to rise in a crisis, just when spreading matters most.
This guide explains how diversification works; it does not say how any portfolio should be built.
Trading costs and minimum lot sizes make very wide spreading costly for small amounts.

carry-rolldown.title: Carry and roll-down
carry-rolldown.summary: What a bond earns over time if the yield curve does not move: the income over its funding cost, and the gain as it ages along the curve.
keypoints: Carry is a bond's yield less the cost of funding it.
Roll-down is the price gain as a bond ages and its yield moves down an upward-sloping curve.
Both are estimates for an unchanged curve, stated per year in basis points.
Divided by duration, they put long and short bonds on the same footing.

p: A bond pays its yield for as long as it is owned. Against that stands the cost of the money used: for a dealer, the cost of funding; for a saver, what the money would earn elsewhere. ZinvestIQ uses the 12-month treasury bill yield plus a small margin as the funding rate, so carry is the bond's yield less that rate.

As time passes, a five-year bond becomes a four-and-three-quarter-year bond. If the curve slopes upward and does not move, the bond is now valued at a slightly lower yield, so its price rises a little. That gain, measured over a quarter and stated per year, is the roll-down. On a steep part of the curve it can be large; on a flat part, close to zero.

Long bonds usually show more carry and roll-down, but they also move more when yields change. Dividing carry plus roll-down by duration gives what each bond earns per unit of rate risk, which makes bonds of different lengths comparable.

limits: Everything assumes the curve does not move; any change in yields will usually outweigh carry over a short period.
The funding margin is an assumption, and each investor's own cost of money differs.
Tax is not modelled.

duration-convexity.title: Duration and convexity
duration-convexity.summary: How much a bond's price changes when yields move, and why the change is not quite a straight line.
keypoints: Modified duration is roughly the percentage price change for a 1% change in yield.
Longer bonds, and bonds with lower coupons, have higher duration.
Convexity measures how the price change bends: prices rise a little more when yields fall than they drop when yields rise by the same amount.
The scenario table on each bond's page applies both to yield moves of different sizes.

p: A bond with a modified duration of 5 loses about 5% of its price if yields rise by one percentage point, and gains about 5% if they fall by one. Duration grows with a bond's remaining life and is larger when its coupon is low, because more of its value comes at the end.

Duration gives a straight-line estimate. The true relationship between price and yield curves upward, so for large moves the price gains a little more when yields fall, and loses a little less when they rise, than duration alone says. Convexity measures that curvature; it matters most for long bonds and large yield moves.

Each bond's page applies its duration and convexity to yield moves of different sizes and shows the estimated price after each. It answers the question: if yields moved by this much, roughly where would this bond's price be?

limits: The estimates assume the whole curve moves by the same amount; in practice short and long yields often move differently.
They are approximations; for very large moves the full price calculation differs slightly.
A bond kept to maturity repays its face value whatever the path of its price.

getting-started.title: How to start investing in Sri Lanka
getting-started.summary: The practical first steps: the accounts you need, where each kind of investment is bought, what it costs, and how much you need to begin.
keypoints: A fixed deposit needs only a bank account; treasury bills and bonds go through a bank or a primary dealer; shares need a share account (CDS) opened through a stockbroker.
Opening a CDS account needs your NIC, proof of address and bank details, and is done through any licensed stockbroker.
Costs matter for small amounts: each share trade pays about 1.1 % in fees, both when shares are bought and when they are disposed of.
Unit trusts let small amounts be spread over many shares or bonds at once, through a fund manager.

sections.h: First, the order most people take
p: Before any investment, most people keep money for emergencies somewhere they can reach quickly, such as a savings account or a short fixed deposit. Only money that can be left alone for years is usually put into shares, because share prices can fall and stay down for a long time.
Government treasury bills and bonds sit in between: they pay a known rupee return if kept to the end, and can be reached earlier only at the market's price.

Offered by licensed commercial banks and licensed finance companies. A deposit needs a bank account and an identity document; the rate is fixed for the term. Deposits at licensed institutions are covered by the Sri Lanka Deposit Insurance Scheme up to a limit per depositor and institution; the current limit is published by the Central Bank.

The government issues them at regular auctions. Individuals usually take part through a primary dealer or a bank, which bids at the auction or offers from its own stock; each sets its own minimum amount. The securities are held in your name in the central depository for government securities (LankaSecure). The bonds pages on this site show the yields dealers quote each day.

sections.h: Shares on the Colombo Stock Exchange
p: Shares are held in a Central Depository System (CDS) account, opened through a stockbroker that is a member of the CSE; the CSE publishes the list. The broker asks for your NIC, proof of address and bank details. Orders are placed through the broker, by phone or in its trading app; shares settle into your CDS account and money into your bank account.
There is no official minimum, but each trade pays fees of about 1.1 % of its value (brokerage, exchange and regulator fees), so very small, frequent trades lose a noticeable share to costs.

A unit trust pools many investors' money and invests it in shares, bonds or deposits, run by a fund manager licensed by the Securities and Exchange Commission. It is one way to own a spread of investments with a small amount; the fund charges a yearly fee.

ZinvestIQ does not take orders or look after anyone's money. It shows what the markets are doing and explains how to read them, so that whichever way you choose to invest, you understand what you are looking at.

limits: Fees, minimums and procedures change; check them with the bank, dealer or broker before acting.
This guide describes how each route works; it does not say which suits anyone.
